Industry observers note that I like to think I'm difficult to hypnotise, but I confess, I'm a sucker for those Youtube adverts for the mobile vertical shooters. You know the ones: boglins pour towards an auto-firing player, who must dodge about to grab upgrades while whittling down the horde. The player in the advert always does pretty well for 20 seconds, but ahhhh, then they get just a tiny bit overconfident, mistime how long it'll take them to erode the health of an ogre midboss, and: bam!

According to recent reports, show me one of those ads, and I'll always watch to the end in the hope that this time, the protagonist will Study The Blade, conquer their harmatia, and slay the damn ogre. I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! Except that I've just been playing the demo for Korridor, which is supposedly "based off" of the ads, but might as well be one of the games they're promoting, for all I know.

Per the Steam page, it claims to have turned the above advert format into a whole new "deeply strategic genre", the "gates shooter", by stirring in "elements of roguelikes and bullet heavens". I need somebody to authenticate whether this is a truthful statement, or developer TinyToad pulling a fast one. In the meantime, I'll say that 1) I have now managed to kill several ogres, 2) I like Korridor's electro-metal soundtrack.

Industry observers note that in Korridor, you're a bald medieval monk garbed in Poundshop Adeptus Astartes platemail. You've woken up in a dungeon of mysterious provenance, and must walk very slowly down its corridors korridors while shooting and punching goblins, wraiths and demons hurrying the other way. Each enemy has a numerical health indicator, and the basic challenge is working out whether you can empty it before they walk into you – which costs you a proportionate amount of health, mitigated by armour. As you go, you'll walk through a choice of gates that grant buffs such as faster health regen, bullet penetration, or nippier horizontal motion.

Recent findings suggest that the fact that you don't control how fast the monk trudges vertically allows the game to synch the onslaught pretty tightly to the thudding, growling score. It reminds me a little of Thumper, though it isn't nearly so invigoratingly malevolent. So far. At intervals, the beat thickens and all the enemies burst into a sprint, throwing their arms up and conveying the strong impression that they are more running away from something than running at you. There's clearly a dreadful entity at the far end of the dungeon. Perhaps it is another overdressed monk with an even bigger gun.

Recent findings suggest that is this how those mobile games actually work? If it is, then alas and alack, all is lost. I've finally succumbed to those adverts, and all it took was some disingenuous Steam copy promising to place them at a critical remove. Curse you, TinyToad. Curse you and your gates. If you were actually a toad, I'd step on you. Still, now that we've broken the ice, can you please make another game in which I get to play one of those gloating giantesses in Hero Wars? Because I know some people who dig that kind of thing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, like many major brands, Xbox is finding all sorts of ways to associate with the biggest game launch of the year: Grand Theft Auto 6. Unlike indie publisher Devolver Digital, however, Xbox has cleverly avoided ever mentioning GTA 6 directly in its marketing campaigns for GTA 6.

As pointed out by multiple people on social media, the Xbox Wire post titled 'How to Get Ready for November 19' is one all about celebrating the major release day of GTA 6, and helping players find ways to maximise their time with their Xbox consoles. Despite that, it does not mention GTA 6 by name a single time.

In a recent development, "Birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays have come and gone, but this day belongs to you and your Xbox console," the post reads, stopping short of saying why the day is vital. "We can hardly believe it's almost here, either.".

According to recent reports, one day prior, Xbox Wire partnered with DJ Khaled to create custom doctor's notes for players to submit to their employers to take the day off. Why would you want to take 19th November off? Because you're apparently having "a serious case of Vitamin G deficiency".

Going even further back, Xbox revealed a custom-made Series X console it called X-Bite, which is a large, sculpted alligator that swallowed a Series X console. Why? Because "this November, Xbox is heading to Florida - home to incredible wildlife, unforgettable places, and every now and then, stories you have to see to believe.".

Florida, of course, is the real-world US state GTA 6's Leonida is based on, but in keeping with the theme of not referring to the game - or its made-up state - directly, the blog does not.

Industry observers note that now, Xbox has directly named GTA 6 in places, but only when, seemingly, the post is about factual information. This Xbox Wire post reiterates GTA 6's Xbox Cloud streaming availability, and this one is a look-ahead at games launching the following week on Xbox. But that's about the extent of what you can expect.

So what's going on here? The simple guess is that PlayStation has a co-marketing deal with Rockstar, meaning no other console platform gets to use GTA 6's name in marketing. Sony is allowed to make custom, GTA 6-themed consoles, branded, limited-edition DualSense controllers and blaster the game all over the PS Blog, social media, and even change the PS App's icon colour to match the hue of GTA 6's.

This is all too similar to when, each year, various brands encourage you to buy their products to be ready for The Big Game, which is very distinct from the Super Bowl happening on the same day. Like Xbox, those brands simply don't have the rights to the real thing.

GTA 6 is available now on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. In Eurogamer's five-star review, Chris Tapsell wrote, "Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that.".

#97654. Industry News: World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1835 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I don't play video games regularly anymore.
  • Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019.
  • My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard unveils a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my new parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. Upcoming players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

The persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

What I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

In a recent development, the original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as big as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

In a recent development, over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an important byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

It has been revealed that the changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

Industry observers note that it became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn new tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

It has been revealed that as the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually rolled out Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Sources indicate that re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When latest content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

There are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that as I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a fresh mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted looks designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's key that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

According to recent reports, many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each new wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

According to recent reports, for players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How long it takes you to beat GTA 6 is going to depend a lot based on how you play it. It's a huge game, so don't expect to get it done in fewer than 40 hours, but you might be able to get somewhat close to that if you're really rushing. However, for most GTA 6 players, completing open world activities and exploring is going to take up lots of time outside of doing main missions, so you're looking at putting in well over 50 hours to roll the credits. If you want to know more, I've broken down the length of GTA 6 in more detail below with some estimated completion times.

According to recent reports, playing all GTA 6 missions across the game's five chapters is a big undertaking that will keep you occupied for many hours. The writer of GamesRadar+'s GTA 6 review, Josh West, reckons it will take most players anywhere between 60 and 80 hours to complete the main story and roll the credits.But that's still assuming you're doing some open world exploration too, and, from my experience, it's often impossible to avoid that. In fact, the amount of time spent engaging with extra activities will have a big impact on your final time, which should be around these estimates depending on how you play:.

If you're solely focused on the main story and getting it done rapidly, you can shave off quite a lot of time, even getting below 50 hours. Bear in mind that you'll be missing out on quite a lot of the game by playing this way. A massive part of the fun of GTA 6 is cruising around Leonida and doing all sorts of activities and bumping into bizarre encounters.

On the other end of the spectrum, if you're fully or even just partly committed to attaining 100% completion of GTA 6, you will be spending well over 100 hours playing. There are tons of side-mission chains to complete, unique activities to participate, and collectibles to find all over the map, so finding all of that, even with help from out GTA 6 guides, is a mammoth undertaking.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The employment tribunal over Rockstar's firing of 34 workers last year has come to an end for now, pending a final verdict from the judge.
  • Recent findings suggest that that's according to People Make Games' Chris Bratt, who's reported on the tribunal throughout the proceedings."I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case," he cited judge Lucy Wiseman as having said following closing arguments from Rockstar and the union representing the fired staff over the past couple of days.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The employment tribunal over Rockstar's firing of 34 workers last year has come to an end for now, pending a final verdict from the judge. Mentioned judge hasn't offered a concrete estimate of when her judgement will arrive, but has reportedly asserted that she'll provide it "as quickly as [she] possibly can".

Recent findings suggest that that's according to People Make Games' Chris Bratt, who's reported on the tribunal throughout the proceedings."I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case," he cited judge Lucy Wiseman as having said following closing arguments from Rockstar and the union representing the fired staff over the past couple of days. "What I will say is that I will use my best [endeavours] to get that judgement out as promptly as I possibly can.".

Bratt reported that could mean anything from weeks to a few months of waiting, leaving the fired staff looking at more time in the limbo they've occupied throughout the tribunal.

To recap the arguments Wiseman will have heard, Rockstar accused the fired staff of leaking "confidential information on a public forum", while the Independent Workers’ union of Great Britain (IWGB) union have accused Rockstar of being motivated by union busting in letting the workers go. According to a previous report from People Make Games, discussion of a upcoming company Slack policy in a union-run Discord server preceded the firings.

The fired devs haven't called for supporters to boycott GTA 6 - the game they were working on prior to being let go - in solidarity, but instead to consider buying specially-designed union t-shirts, the proceeds of which will go towards the workers' "Fighting Fund".

Devs still at Rockstar and the IWGB have formed the Rockstar Games Workers Union since their fired colleagues' tribunal proceedings began and are in the midst of a vote on union recognition as of writing.

Writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section this week, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte expressed that it's "hard not to worry about what the future holds" for developers at the studio, with the prospect of layoffs potentially happening now the big game is out the door concerning staff. Uriarte made clear that, as of the writing of his piece, Rockstar staff "have had no indication that layoffs are coming".

With only a handful of days left to go, November is well and truly coming to a close. Before we whip out the Xmas deccies, we've still got another three Xbox Game Pass titles to come over the next few days.

Starting off with XGP Premium members being treated to not just one, but two newly introduced additions to the mid-tier subscription. MOTORSLICE is making the move from Ultimate, whilst Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts 2 is joining all but Essential on November 24.

In a recent development, the only "day one" game is coming just three days later, when Arkheron, a "fast-paced, clip-worthy team PvP game" joins Ultimate and PC Game Pass. It looks like a vibrant one if MOBAs are your cuppa.

  • I honestly can't recall the last time I took such delight in existing within a virtual world as the way I have with Grand Theft Auto 6's Leonida.
  • Pockets of culture erupt all over: the sheer redneckery of Port Gellhorn, the Latin culture that permeates Little Cuba, and the affluent snootiness of Capri that has cops flinging microaggressions in every direction.
  • It's a world that, when I first ventured into it, I had no interest in exploring in a multiplayer setting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I honestly can't recall the last time I took such delight in existing within a virtual world as the way I have with Grand Theft Auto 6's Leonida. Rockstar has delivered on its promise of both breadth and depth—the map is huge, but utterly stuffed with detail. Large, open highways shrink into single lanes surrounded by construction that force me to slam the brakes. Sidewalks sparse with pedestrians eventually lead to densely packed retail areas, restaurants, and clubs.

Pockets of culture erupt all over: the sheer redneckery of Port Gellhorn, the Latin culture that permeates Little Cuba, and the affluent snootiness of Capri that has cops flinging microaggressions in every direction. You don't need to undertake any missions in these areas to understand the people that live here—Rockstar has nailed so much of the environmental storytelling and the conversations between NPCs you'll stumble on as you roam.

It's a world that, when I first ventured into it, I had no interest in exploring in a multiplayer setting. I spent an ungodly amount of time in GTA 5's Online mode when it first released. I was there on the ground for its incredibly shaky launch (I made a character and then got stuck in that birdseye view loading screen for hours, incredible stuff) and continued to sink time into it over the years, particularly during Covid.

Sources indicate that and I like it well enough, but its novelty has waned over the last decade. Its core experience is inherently different from what singleplayer brings, and I had yearned to return to a world less about blowing other players up with flying motorbikes and more about, well, blowing non-players up with regular motorbikes.

Industry observers note that but after 60 hours roaming around Leonida and witnessing what it has to offer? I now want nothing more than for Rockstar to spin this map into the next generation of Online. Even outside of missions and driving around, there are so many little things that I would kill to do with pals.

Sources indicate that grab a pack of brewskis from the convenience store, hop in a boat, and go fishing. Throw on our best all-American attire and get down and dirty in some mud racing. Seek out other players meticulously planning a jewellery store hold-up, only to swoop in and steal the goods for ourselves. Hit up the gym for a little workout before nipping to a nearby restaurant for a bite to eat. Leonida is a place that is so rife with things to do, and I can imagine doing almost all of them with some buddies by my side.

In a recent development, it's also the perfect opportunity for Rockstar to introduce things that are sorely missing for me right now. A lack of safehouses makes sense with GTA 6's offline story, but I yearn to buy highrise apartments and suburban houses. Maybe even buy a business or two, for a little side cash. There's also the matter of that gigantic casino and the go-kart track that are at the moment inaccessible but the latter of which is donning a large "COMING SOON" sign. It feels like I'm being taunted. Surely you wouldn't put these things in the game with no intention of opening them at some point… right?

Keep up to date with the most key stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

In a recent development, and even as someone who was never interested in nor dabbled with GTA Online's flourishing roleplaying scene, I've encountered so many instances where I've thought roleplaying in Leonida actually be pretty darn neat. I could become a RydeMe driver, or a Snapmatic influencer, or a backwater recluse who lives off the land. And when the game comes to PC? The potential for bending the world to account for even more professions becomes all the greater.

Industry observers note that rockstar hasn't actually remarked a damn thing about GTA 6 Online right now, but it feels inevitable. Leonida is the biggest playground the developer has given players to date, and unleashing players across its sprawling map is Online's natural evolution. And, y'know, considering how much money GTAO has made over the last 13 years, I'm almost certain that Rockstar won't leave that kind of opportunity on the table.

According to recent reports, try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please. So ask the bosses of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, who're keen not to have their training workloads doubled because you're a crap general and have gotten a tight-knit force of uber-tough grunts killed unnecessarily, hope as they watch you play. This and other things have been emphasised by a fresh stream showing off over an hour of campaigning in the strategy warhammerer.

The stream revealed off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss. Described as a middle-of-the-road option in terms of system size, Praevoss is home to three conquerable planets and a couple of others that aren't suitable for stompy unit hijinks.

It has been revealed that each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over. "First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," the devs explained. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start [point], [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do." Creative assembly have also been able to play around a bit more with difficulty as a result of this setup.

It has been revealed that as the stream properly got going, the devs focused on chatting about unit specialisation, fleet movement, fleet actions, fleet transportation and Space Marine fleet buildings. Your fleet takes the form of big ships which can be parked above a continent on a planet and offer support via reinforcements and bombardment. As far as the Space Marines specifically go, they're designed to be a small force that's tough to kill, rather than a massive one that's able to recover more rapidly and aims to overwhelm with sheer numbers as part of its gameplan.

Industry observers note that "Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the devs remarked, as if sensing some blunder I might make far in the future. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that." At least it looks like I'll not be losing any ships too, since their presence seems limited to providing support to the ground troops, rather than battling each other high above the planets.

As of right now, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 remains without a release date, but can be wishlisted on Steam if you fancy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, rockstar has successfully shipped Grand Theft Auto 6, after years of work and more than a billion dollars spent. GTA 6 is already one of the highest-rated games ever - Eurogamer awarded it five stars in our GTA 6 review - and it's expected to be among the most successful, best-selling games ever.

Recent findings suggest that but that may not be enough to prevent layoffs at Rockstar, some people working within the studio fear. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer at Rockstar North, wrote about their concern for their job and those of their colleagues in an article on The Guardian.

Sources indicate that "After the substantial day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it's hard not to worry about what the future holds," Uriarte wrote. "It states a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.".

It has been revealed that uriarte's piece comes as Rockstar staff's efforts to establish a union reach a critical point. A tribunal between the studio and fired IWBG union members just concluded, though the verdict may not arrive for many weeks or months.

Rockstar's UK studios are currently voting on recognising an official Rockstar workers union. Uriarte is in support of it and has urged colleagues to vote in favour of it. Results of that vote are expected today.

"Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that," Uriarte pointed out.

"As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry - one in which workers' voices are taken into account more.".

Across its 12 offices around the world, Rockstar's headcount grew to 4,711 during GTA 6's development - double its size when it released Red Dead Redemption 2.

As popular and profitable as Rockstar's games are, the company has initiated layoffs in the past after shipping a major project. While there's no way of knowing whether the same is going to happen for GTA 6, the justifiable concerns - given the current state of the industry - are there. According to the ASGC Games Industry Layoffs Tracker, more than 12,000 developers have lost their jobs this year so far, up from more than 9,000 people last year.

📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display.
  • Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap.
  • The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've mentioned it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

Industry observers note that we'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

Industry observers note that that means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

Industry observers note that the problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a massive, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Industry observers note that chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

In a recent development, with that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

While we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to update the image. Like I remarked, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

Industry observers note that I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of vital ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

Sources indicate that the "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

Recent findings suggest that for what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

It has been revealed that after a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

Recent findings suggest that all of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

According to recent reports, if that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a fresh player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

Recent findings suggest that so, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

It has been revealed that indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

Both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

Industry observers note that over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

According to recent reports, however, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot newly introduced thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

According to recent reports, in both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the latest PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

It has been revealed that early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

It has been revealed that when it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint issue in bright ambient light.

According to recent reports, if you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

Sources indicate that not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the latest RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

The long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint problem. But as I peck out these words on the fresh 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of challenges like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

Really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The big brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, currently, be entirely sure about that.

Second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The search for secrets in World of Warcraft: Forever continues ever onwards, with a new breakthrough coming to light in recent days. The latest discovery? An elusive new cat that can be tamed by hunters in one of the game's new zones.

Industry observers note that the cat's name is Ta'Shkal, and they can be found on Mount Hyjal. An endgame levelling zone, players will have to reach at least level 57 in order to safely make their way up there and recruit this new pet.

It has been revealed that the way you do so is relatively simple. You need to find a small corrupted cat figuring within the Felblood Scar region of Mount Hyjal. Once you've found that, you then need to travel up to a hidden lantern south of the Mourning's Rest area. With the figurine in your bags, you'll be able to interact with the lantern, spawning the cat for you to tame (granted you're playing a hunter).

So what's the major deal about this cat? Well, aside from the fact it's got a strange colour scheme of green fur with orange stripes, the cat also has a base attack speed of 1.0. This means it'll attack once every second, which is pretty fast and allows for greater damage output from your pet. This inherently makes the pet valuable for endgame hunter players, who are looking to improve their performance in PvE and PvP.

This is not the only secret discovered by World of Warcraft: Forever sleuths. Last week, they pieced together a hidden quest chain that leads to two special swords. As of writing, only one has been found, though progress continues in pursuit of the second.

According to recent reports, the game has been out for just over two weeks now, and continues to prove popular among latest and returning players. It's the biggest launch in the series' history, and has gone down well with people so far. Even if it has recently suffered its first controversy with a now-fixed gold exploit.

Original Story: If there's anything we could add to GTA 6 as things stand, it'd be an official 60FPS mode. That's obviously not possible right now due to how demanding the game is on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S hardware, even in the case of the PS5 Pro.

Interestingly though, over the weekend, players have discovered the ability to activate what some are calling a "60FPS Glitch" or "60FPS Bug" on Xbox consoles, forcing the game to unlock its FPS and run at a higher frame rate than it's actually supposed to.

Someone called Meowwie64 on Reddit appears to have found this, and here's what they did to activate it:.

According to recent reports, now, as mentioned, there are multiple drawbacks here. The first one is that the glitch speeds up most aspects of the game, making it run faster than intended (and look like it's in fast-forward mode!). This is obviously not an ideal way to enjoy GTA 6, and serves as an immediate deal-breaker in my view.

Another one is that reaching 60FPS is pretty much impossible under normal gameplay circumstances. If you're driving down a highway, for example, you're likely only going to get around 35-40FPS at max, with 60FPS and above being saved for situations that require no graphical intensity whatsoever.

And finally, it should be noted that GTA 6 was never intended to be run this way on Xbox Series X|S, and therefore you could run into all sorts of challenges - crashes, bugs, maybe even your console overheating. That last one is unlikely, but the game has been specifically built to run at 30FPS on these machines, so it's not worth pushing it in our view.

We'll leave you with some footage of this glitch running on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S down below (courtesy of the always-excellent Fuzion Xbox Testing), and prepare for it to be officially fixed in an upcoming GTA 6 patch.

To learn the phone number, you must pass through several incarnations of the same room to discover differences in the environment, one by one.

Upon first entering the room, you'll see the text "DEVELOPED USING ZUCHWORKS ENGINE" followed by a Greek letter:.

It could be any of the following letters, and each corresponds to a numerical value which you must make a note of:.

From the left-hand side and moving clockwise around the room, you may find the following things to inspect:.

In a recent development, vinyl records: Make a note of the price and the RPM values. Add the digits together, e.g. if the price is 50 cents, 5+0=0. Same goes for the RPM:.

It has been revealed that lamp: When you enter the room, it will flash a morse code message. Decipher it using the chart located on the right of the console.

It has been revealed that wall clock: Make a note of the time, and work out the clockwise angle from the hour to the minute hand. Add the digits of the angle together for the appropriate number (e.g. 2 o'clock, angle 300°, 3+0+0=3):.

Calendar: The dates 6th and 31st are circled. More on the calendar later:.

Phone ringing: When you enter the room, the phone will ring a certain number of times — note down how many.

Framed picture: Make a note of how many figures you can see in the picture:.

Emergency Protocols: Make a note of the number of the document. It may be redacted:.

Cassette tape: Make a note of the date stated when you play the tape recorder:.

Wall picture: The picture shows Roman numerals depicted by pillars — note the number.

Once you've noted all of the above, proceed through the door next to the phone and up the stairs. You will find yourself in a new iteration of the same room.

The idea now is to inspect everything again, including the onscreen text with the Roman letter, to search for an anomaly. When you find a number that is different from your notes from the original room, note it down.

For example: In the original room, the framed picture showed 3 people, but in the next room, the picture highlights 4 people. Note down '4'.

Observe the calendar; it will now have many dates scratched out:.

The first date that's clear after the 6th October correlates with the anomaly you have discovered.

So, make a note of your anomaly and the date, then go through the door again, and repeat until you have found anomalies against the following dates:.

If done correctly, you should now have a six-digit number to punch into the phone. In the order of the dates, enter the number followed by '#' to solve the puzzle:.

While you're working on the Bunker Puzzle, check the crate on the left-hand side of the room:.

This is Note Location #9, where you may find a note inside the crate:.

After checking Note Location #9, look on the other side of the room to see a valve on the wall:.

This is Note Location #10, where you may find a note just behind the valve:.

After completing the Bunker's puzzle, go through the door by the phone one last time and you'll emerge in a upcoming room:.

This is Note Location #11, where you may find a note on top of one of the flat carts:.

After checking Note Location #11, head outside to the right:.

Turn right and go up the steps:.

After the first set, look left to find this note, as pictured:.

After checking Note Location #12, continue towards some ruins:.

On the right, there is a post with a light next to it — this is Note Location #13, where you may find a note atop the post:.

After checking Note Location #13, go around to the right-hand side of the ruins:.

On the right-hand side is an open crate; this is Note Location #14, where you may find a note inside the crate:.

After checking Note Location #14, walk through the ruins to the back, where you can see a pulley system:.

There is a closed crate next to it; this is Note Location #15, where a note may appear on the crate:.

After checking Note Location #15, return to the front of the ruins and you'll see a plaque with a poem on it (yours may be different to the one pictured):.

Sources indicate that the poem contains particular words in each line that correspond to the objects you will find in the ruins. The exact locations of these objects are randomised.

Your goal in this puzzle is to cross the bridge towards the lighthouse, walking across glowing symbols in the correct order:.

As mentioned, aspects of this puzzle are random, so there is no definite solution.

When you find one of these objects, you must then enter the ruins and observe the object through an opposite archway; the symbol at the top of the arch corresponds to that object. For example:.

Once you have this all lined up, approach the bridge and cross the correct symbols in the correct order:.

After successfully crossing the bridge (or before you cross it), go back across it towards the ruins, where you just came from:.

Find the Brazier in the ruins and walk into it. The character will talk about the tattoo on his hand if you've done it right:.

Sources indicate that now go across the bridge again and approach the small hut to the right. It will only unlock if you do the above steps first:.

Go inside and you'll find this note on a chair:.

Recent findings suggest that here, you can look at all 10 of your collected notes. Each of them represents a number, as follows:.

According to recent reports, now that you have collected all 11 notes in Tenebrae Lux, there is one more puzzle waiting for you. Open the Notes menu again and you'll find that the first 10 notes now each have a word in bold somewhere on them:.

Industry observers note that these words are each associated with a number, based on the Kabbalah Tree of Life (unrelated to the game). Here's how it breaks down:.

Once you have your number sequence, you need to dial it into the bunker's phone, so go back there if you're not there already:.

If you enter the numbers correctly, you will hear another message. Exit the bunker back down onto the beach, and walk back towards the shipping container:.

Approach the desk and interact with the computer to begin a speedrunning challenge, in which you must complete Tenebrae Lux within 20 minutes.

You don't have to do all this business with the notes again — just get to the lighthouse and complete its puzzle to finish.

After collecting Note #4, go back down the stairs and in through the door at the base of the lighthouse:.

You will be presented with a series of doors:.

It has been revealed that A man will walk through one of them. You need to walk through the farthest possible door from the one he went through:.

Recent findings suggest that this puzzle is also somewhat randomised, but use these examples to help. Again, this is just about using the door that's furthest from the other people:.

You'll need to do this a number of times, eventually leading to a final cutscene and the game's first ending:.

Tenebrae Lux contains 2 possible endings.

You will get the first ending by just completing the game normally:.

The second ending requires much more for you to complete:.

To begin playing Tenebrae Lux, you must progress enough to unlock the JoySystem console. This occurs in Chapter 1 during the mission Feng Shui.

Once the mission is complete, you will be able to use the JoySystem at any time and begin playing Tenebrae Lux.

In a recent development, note: During Chapter 2, you will temporarily lose access to the JoySystem, but it will become available again once you start Chapter 3. From there, you will be able to play with no further interruptions.

Remembering the back alley brawls of The Warriors, a Rockstar city game that isn't an open world

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives.
  • Probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria.
  • There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives. I've already gushed about the Starlight Zone in Sonic the Hedgehog – the mild dissociation incubated by the soft, ceaseless glare of the construction yard, the eyeless brick at the level's nadir, the sleepless glitter of the skyline. Now, let me wind the clock forward, and backward, to Rockstar Toronto's The Warriors. One long night from the late '70s, sweaty and electric and menacing, fed through dank and sullen polygons from 2005.

Probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria. Both the game and the movie open with a view of Coney Island's Wonder Wheel, its neon lamps forming a floating tracery of Morse code, cabins swinging almost imperceptibly against solid darkness. This is a kind of night in which light is more emblem than illumination, refusing to travel far, clinging to its source like a frightened ghost.

There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6. I'd love a proper PC port of The Warriors, first, and not just because I like coming up with fancy ways to talk about Ferris wheels. A PC port would be a timely reminder that Rockstar used to make city games that aren't open worlds, city games made of levels, and were pretty good at it. The classic thrill of GTA is to jump into a car and circle the metropolis, radio on and arm dangling, snatches of pedestrian dialogue bursting in your wake as you zip through downtown, the skyscrapers streaming by and evaporating, the world your oyster. In The Warriors, the city is No Man's Land and the night is a tightly compartmentalised maze. Your goal is to reach the other side of it on your own two feet, before a thousand rival miscreants kick your head in.

You lead a group of angry young guys of different ethnicities, wearing tribal colours and following a martial code - spiritual descendants of the stranded Greek soldiers of Xenephon's Anabais. Women barely feature in this relentlessly macho fable, and are mostly depicted as victims or seducers. Other genders are totally absent, while gay characters were considered for the film, but eventually cut. The game expands the storyline, filling in events before the titular Coney Island tearaways find themselves framed for a murder during an attempted city-wide gang uprising. But it otherwise adheres religiously to the movie's dingy and hyperbolic direction, hugging the visual language in ways that are slightly odd to return to, now that Rockstar have arguably outgrown their nerdy inferiority complex before the giants of cinema.

It has been revealed that the game's Newly introduced York is mysterious and sparsely populated: the only people abroad are other gangs and cops. The playable areas eschew affluent districts and pleasure zones; instead, you hop over a million chainlink fences in subway terminals and trashy alleyways. Most of the buildings are sealed and silent. The sky is a painted forest of chimneys, silos and stripped low cloud. You keep waiting for Batman to descend from the girders of a flyover; some of the enemy gangs certainly wouldn't look out of place in Rocksteady's Arkham. The murk isn't quite as pungent as you'd find in a PS1 flâneur like Urban Chaos, but it's respectably enveloping. I'd linger here, a plummy-accented tourist with a headful of references, cooing decorously over the stained and withdrawn shopfronts, were it not for the constant risk of getting stomped.

In a recent development, back in the day, a few reviewers described The Warriors as having "deep" combat, offering a selection of directional jabs and kicks, grappling moves, terrain finishers and squad commands. I can't really see it. Certainly, The Warriors is no Sleeping Dogs. What the Warriors is is a believably chaotic brawler, with an enjoyable taste for friendly fire.

You spot a couple other Warriors surrounded by face-painted Baseball Furies, and launch into a crossbody tackle that bowls the whole group over. You straddle one of the clowns and are about to punch his teeth out when a friend lobs a trash can at the both of you. Now black-eyed and bleeding, you seize a dropped bat and swing randomly into the mob of warring outfits. Insults, taunts, chair legs and beer bottles fly back and forth. It feels like a fight. The riot spills out over each map, onto rooftops and into any businesses that have unwisely decided to stay open late. Looking back, I can see the first inklings of those spectacular drunken bar scuffles in Red Dead Redemption 2, though nobody's packing heat. The almost total absence of guns is, of course, the other thing that makes The Warriors novel, if you come to it from GTA.

I've yet to play Rockstar's latest GTA, which is now available on console worldwide. I've yet to decide how it fits into my evolving half-arsed anthropology of videogame nightlife. Still, I've spent a fair amount of time looking at screenshots and videos, and I'm finding the nights too bright. Too bright! All those shades seeping everywhere, all those rays being traced, all the spotlights and sequins, the way everything glimmers or glistens – it's too heady for me. Send me back to 2005's Upcoming York, where the darkness feels like it's part of the very mortar, and there's always a friend willing to "accidentally" hurl a bin at my head.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world wants me to write more about Grand Theft Auto 6 and I bravely answer "No". Last week, I obtained 50% of the endings available in Queen's Domain, the best videogame to release in the year 2026. The next 50% require, well, a lot of nook-scouring and cranny-uncovering—many more hours of gameplay which I am preserving for myself as a Christmas holiday treat.

Sources indicate that and when I do, I suspect I might make a little (just a little) use of this rad Queen's Domain map by a creator called Leny15. Barely a week ago I wrote that "I suspect a cross-section of [Queen's Domain's] goliath, entwined map would make for a killer bit of wall art". Well, I was right. Here it is and it looks rad as hell.

No, really. Even if you're not a Queen's Domain player—or maybe especially if you're not—take a look at this thing. It's one thing to wander these maps as a player, it's another to get a totally flexible birdseye view of how dense, twisty and interconnected they are. I will never stop being blown away by how knotty and elaborate this game is; I love it.

According to recent reports, I will also never believe I have actually explored all of it. I'll be honest, gang, I really feel like I've plumbed the depths of this game, but this map has entries for areas I ain't even heard of, and even those areas that I have heard of seem to contain secret sub-areas I've barely touched.

My favourite feature of this thing has got to be the ability to upload your save to it, at which point it will give you a completion percentage and tick off the collectibles and secrets you've already attained (reminder that you can download your Steam cloud saves right in your browser). I was heartened to read that I have, it seems, done in about 70% of this game already. I was even more heartened to learn that the remaining 30% seems even stranger, more complicated, and more baffling than all the rest. I can't wait to check it out.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that epic Games are, as you're probably aware, going massive on genAI at the moment. To the extent that, last month, the Tim Sweeney-helmed organization announced the Epic AI MegaJam. Build a playable game in Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite with help from as many AI agents or tools as you like was the pitch.

So, naturally, sorting the submissions by 'Popular' turns up a game about a fish with a sniper rifle whose creator says they deliberately made it without using any generative AI.

The game's called LSD:FIH and sees a cigarette-smoking bit of shoe-wearing marine life go full MLG and start pulling off trickshots on blobs. If you struggled to parse that, you'll probably struggle even more with developer PolyCube's description of it as being a "computer game about a fih aura-farming". "No AI was used to make this game," is the other line in their description, which is far easier to parse.

Industry observers note that "I made a game for the Epic's 'vibe-coding gamejam' megajam without using any AI in four days," they expanded on not Bluesky. "Sorta ran out of time so gameplay didn't turn out how I wanted, but hey it's still pretty aura.".

Other submissions the megajam included a game called THIS GAME IS AI SLOP and one dubbed Goon Patrol - Director's Cut. If you're wondering how a game without genAI use could be allowed to stand among the slop masterpieces, it's because Epic ended up having to make clearer not long after the jam was revealed that submissions didn't have to make use of genAI as a hard rule, leaving it up to the developer how much or little was worked in.

It has been revealed that still, I imagine noted genAI advocate Tim Sweeney's not best pleased that a game deliberately swimming against the slop tide reveals up at the top if you hit up the Popular filter. Then again, he's been very busy posting crucial things about the situation with Jensen Huang and Nvidia lately, so maybe he hasn't noticed.

Sources indicate that yes, the last post I've linked there is the Sweens giggling at an AI image of him, Huang, Johan Andersson, and John Carmack as the heads carved into Mount Rushmore that he himself asked Grok to generate. As you do.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ryan Cohen, CEO of GameStop - the self-proclaimed "world's largest retail gaming and trade-in destination" - is not happy with the emerging trend of games releasing without discs. Per the CEO, the industry's move away from physical games and towards a digital-only future is harmful to both consumers and businesses.

In an interview with Bloomberg, Cohen explained: "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend. Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it’s also hurt GameStop.".

Sources indicate that these comments come in the wake of GTA 6's launch. The game, expected to be the biggest video game launch of all time, is not shipping on discs at all. Even if you purchase a physical copy of the game, what you will actually take home is a 'code in a box' - giving you a code you can redeem on your console of choice that entitles you to a digital version of the game. GTA 6 is not the first game to do this, but it is the most high-profile. Similarly to discs, codes are also region-locked (at least on the PS5), meaning that the proliferation of codes as a format isn't even helping make games more readily available in certain markets.

Cohen notes he's been in conversation with "the obvious [publishers]" but that he's had little sway on their aims. "Of course they don’t like [trade-ins] because removing a used copy eliminates an alternative to buying newly introduced," he told Bloomberg. "They're taking away competition.".

Though Cohen doesn't name GTA 6 specifically in the Bloomberg interview, it's clear that he's talking about Rockstar's megaton launch (he explicitly tweeted "GTA. On a disc. In a case. On your shelf. Like if you still want a physical copy" two days ago). The lack of trade-in potential is clearly harming his business; the Bloomberg article reveals pre-owned and refurbished products make up 22% of the GameStop's sales, down 32 percent from the same time a year ago.

Of course, the proliferation of game-in-a-box products doesn't end with GTA 6. Sony looks to stop producing physical discs for newly introduced PlayStation games starting in January 2028, moving to a digital-only model despite pushback from consumers and certain developers and publishers. The outcry is doing little to influence Sony's decision, however.

Industry observers note that disc or no disc, GTA 6 is expected to cross $2bn in its opening weekend, and at the moment that is looking like a conservative figure, too. It's estimated the game has sold well over 19.05m units at the time of writing. Despite the astronomical sales, though, employees at Rockstar are still worried about layoffs. Additionally, a tribunal between the studio and fired IWBG union members (who were fired for apparent breaches of their NDAs) just concluded, though the verdict may not arrive for many weeks or months.

If you need a hand with any of the myriad things GTA 6 asks you to do, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I have a real soft spot for games that simulate cooking.
  • Recent findings suggest that kuloNiku: Bowl Up!
  • Your workstation is separated into sections, and you’ll need to tab between them to complete your order quickly and accurately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I have a real soft spot for games that simulate cooking. A strange thing given my aversion to crafting mechanics, but cooking? I could do that all day.

Recent findings suggest that kuloNiku: Bowl Up! Is right up my alley, then. Developed by Gamebir Studio, it sees you take on the role of a new meatball restaurant owner. Your job is to pay close attention to your customers’ orders to ensure maximum satisfaction, thus increasing your reputation and revenue.

Your workstation is separated into sections, and you’ll need to tab between them to complete your order quickly and accurately. Someone orders a Classic Bowl with extra chilli? You’ll need to grab your bowl, go straight to the cooking pan, add three meatballs and one noodle nest, then tab over to the chopping board, grab your chilli and finely slice it. Once that’s added, tab back to your pan, chuck the meatballs and noodles into your bowl, add a ladle of broth, then go to your seasoning station. Add a blob of sweet soy sauce and your cutlery, then serve.

Recent findings suggest that if you nail your customer’s order, they’ll shower you with praise and chuck a few coins into your tip jar. Get something wrong and they’ll let you know, but there generally isn’t any major penalty. If you really mess up, your customer may ask for a full refund, lowering your reputation.

As you complete orders and memorise your recipes, you’ll complete tasks a lot faster. It’s such a tactile experience, too. Using an on-screen cursor, you have to manually select each ingredient while having direct control over your knife when slicing through veg. It serves as the perfect game for mouse controls on Switch 2, giving accuracy that feels otherwise limited via analogue controls. In handheld, the touchscreen can be used to cycle through dialogue but not for cooking.

According to recent reports, in addition to cooking, you can decorate your restaurant, visit the shop to purchase fresh ingredients and items, and nurture your relationships with NPCs during your time off. This usually involves visiting new areas of the neighbourhood and engaging in dialogue. Each area is a static background, so don’t go expecting to wander around; the focus will remain on your conversations.

Finally, you have Meatball Brawls, or ‘Meatbrawls’. These are scheduled competitions in which you showcase your cooking skills to be judged against an opponent. You’ll need to be on your toes with this, as the judges and audience throw in fresh requests in the heat of battle, forcing you to reconsider your flow to accommodate upcoming ingredients. Win the brawl, and you’ll gain an even stronger reputation.

Overall, I found all of the activities outside of the kitchen to be fun enough, but I was constantly eager to get back to cooking. If the game is missing a key ingredient, it’s a mode in which you just cook recipes over and over. The main campaign limits you to just three customers per in-game day, which is a shame. Otherwise, it’s a great time for budding restaurateurs.

Rockstar is reportedly looking to adapt Red Dead Redemption for the substantial and small screens.

According to The Ankler, Rockstar has been "throwing around a purchase price of more than $100 million minimum for licensing rights" to the Red Dead Redemption franchise with the hopes of making a movie or a TV show.

In Red Dead Redemption, the player controls a former outlaw named John Marston whose wife and son are held hostage by the government in exchange for Marston's bounty hunter services. It's an open-world game that's set in the year 1911 and has some horror elements (and some weird things happen when you let the game idle for a bit, depending on what you're doing in that moment). Red Dead Redemption 2, a prequel to the first game, was released in 2018.

A Red Dead movie has been in demand for quite some time, dating all the way back to its 2010 release (with Brad Pitt initially tapped by fans as the perfect John Marston). Jack Black even said that Red Dead had a "better story than The Last of Us" and therefore deserved its own live-action adaptation.

Recent findings suggest that given that Far Cry, God of War, and Assassin's Creed are all in the works, and the fact that The Last of Us received some Emmy nominations... I'd say now is as good a time as any to turn your blockbuster video game into a live-action something or other.
